claim: Retinal diseases such as Stargardt disease, age-related macular degeneration, diabetic retinopathies or retinitis pigmentosa are amongst the leading causes of vision loss in humans.
source: Retinal diseases such as Stargardt disease, age-related macular degeneration, diabetic retinopathies or retinitis pigmentosa are amongst the leading causes of vision loss in humans (Croze et al., 2014; Buch et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Croze et al., 2014; Buch et al., 2004).

claim: There are currently no cures available for retinal diseases such as Stargardt disease, age-related macular degeneration, diabetic retinopathies or retinitis pigmentosa.
source: Unfortunate for patients suffering from those diseases, there are currently no cures available (Shintani et al., 2009; Fine et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Shintani et al., 2009; Fine et al., 2000).

claim: The complex neuro-retinal organization and the vast blood-supply make retinal tissue susceptible for side effects of compounds delivered intravitreally or systemically.
source: Moreover, the complex neuro-retinal organization and the vast blood-supply make retinal tissue susceptible for side effects of compounds delivered intravitreally or systemically (Penha et al., 2010; Renouf et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Penha et al., 2010; Renouf et al., 2012).

claim: Retinal toxicities are a major issue for a wide range of therapeutic substances, especially for targeted anticancer agents since many of the targets are also expressed in ocular tissues.
source: Retinal toxicities are a major issue for a wide range of therapeutic substances, especially for targeted anticancer agents since many of the targets are also expressed in ocular tissues (Renouf et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Renouf et al., 2012).

claim: Animal models fail to reflect fundamental characteristics of human vision including trichromacy or a fovea centralis, responsible for high visual acuity.
source: Although animal models that are used to explore new therapeutic options and assess retinal toxicities resemble the human (patho-)physiology of vision in certain aspects, they fail to reflect fundamental characteristics including trichromacy or a fovea centralis, responsible for high visual acuity (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1 which illustrates the limitations of animal models.

claim: Retinal organoids (ROs) resemble rudimentary optic vesicle-like structures with a retinal layering similar to in vivo conditions.
source: Retinal organoids (ROs), also called 'eyes in the dish', resemble rudimentary optic vesicle-like structures with a retinal layering similar to in vivo conditions (Nakano et al., 2012; Zhong et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Nakano et al., 2012; Zhong et al., 2014).

claim: Retinal organoids contain most relevant retinal cell types in a physiological layering such as ganglion cells, amacrine cells, horizontal cells, bipolar cells, Müller glia as well as rods and cones.
source: These ROs contain most relevant retinal cell types in a physiological layering such as ganglion cells, amacrine cells, horizontal cells, bipolar cells, Müller glia as well as rods and cones.
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of RO composition in the manuscript and is further supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: hPSC-ROs lack functional maturation of differentiated cells.
source: Some of the major hurdles are (i) the functional maturation of differentiated cells, (ii) lack of essential cell types (e.g. microglia), (iii) lack of a physiological interplay of the various retinal cell types especially of photoreceptors and retinal pigment epithelia (RPE), as well as (iv) a missing vascularization (reviewed in Achberger et al., 2019; Yin et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to review articles (Achberger et al., 2019; Yin et al., 2016).

claim: hPSC-ROs lack essential cell types such as microglia.
source: Some of the major hurdles are (i) the functional maturation of differentiated cells, (ii) lack of essential cell types (e.g. microglia), (iii) lack of a physiological interplay of the various retinal cell types especially of photoreceptors and retinal pigment epithelia (RPE), as well as (iv) a missing vascularization (reviewed in Achberger et al., 2019; Yin et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to review articles (Achberger et al., 2019; Yin et al., 2016).

claim: hPSC-ROs lack a physiological interplay of the various retinal cell types especially of photoreceptors and retinal pigment epithelia (RPE).
source: Some of the major hurdles are (i) the functional maturation of differentiated cells, (ii) lack of essential cell types (e.g. microglia), (iii) lack of a physiological interplay of the various retinal cell types especially of photoreceptors and retinal pigment epithelia (RPE), as well as (iv) a missing vascularization (reviewed in Achberger et al., 2019; Yin et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to review articles (Achberger et al., 2019; Yin et al., 2016).

claim: hPSC-ROs lack vascularization.
source: Some of the major hurdles are (i) the functional maturation of differentiated cells, (ii) lack of essential cell types (e.g. microglia), (iii) lack of a physiological interplay of the various retinal cell types especially of photoreceptors and retinal pigment epithelia (RPE), as well as (iv) a missing vascularization (reviewed in Achberger et al., 2019; Yin et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to review articles (Achberger et al., 2019; Yin et al., 2016).

claim: The developed retina-on-a-chip (RoC) is a novel microphysiological model of the human retina integrating more than seven different essential retinal cell types derived from hiPSCs.
source: In this study, we present the retina-on-a-chip (RoC), a novel microphysiological model of the human retina integrating more than seven different essential retinal cell types derived from hiPSCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the RoC system in the manuscript and by data showing multiple cell types (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: The RoC provides vasculature-like perfusion.
source: It provides vasculature-like perfusion and enables, for the first time, the recapitulation of the interaction of mature photoreceptor segments with RPE in vitro.
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the microfluidic system and computational fluid dynamics simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: The RoC enables, for the first time, the recapitulation of the interaction of mature photoreceptor segments with RPE in vitro.
source: It provides vasculature-like perfusion and enables, for the first time, the recapitulation of the interaction of mature photoreceptor segments with RPE in vitro.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing the interaction between photoreceptor segments and RPE in the RoC (Figures 6 and 7).

claim: The interaction between photoreceptors and RPE in the RoC enhances the formation of outer segment-like structures.
source: We show that this interaction enhances the formation of outer segment-like structures and the establishment of in vivo-like physiological processes such as outer segment phagocytosis and calcium dynamics.
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data showing increased outer segment formation in the RoC compared to controls (Figure 6h).

claim: The interaction between photoreceptors and RPE in the RoC enables the establishment of in vivo-like physiological processes such as outer segment phagocytosis.
source: We show that this interaction enhances the formation of outer segment-like structures and the establishment of in vivo-like physiological processes such as outer segment phagocytosis and calcium dynamics.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments by RPE cells in the RoC (Figure 7).

claim: The interaction between photoreceptors and RPE in the RoC enables the establishment of in vivo-like physiological processes such as calcium dynamics.
source: We show that this interaction enhances the formation of outer segment-like structures and the establishment of in vivo-like physiological processes such as outer segment phagocytosis and calcium dynamics.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing calcium imaging in the RoC (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: The RoC reproduces the retinopathic side-effects of the anti-malaria drug chloroquine.
source: In addition, we demonstrate the applicability of the RoC for drug testing, by reproducing the retinopathic side-effects of the anti-malaria drug chloroquine and the antibiotic gentamicin.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing increased cell death and lysosomal dysfunction in the RoC after chloroquine treatment (Figure 8a-c).

claim: The RoC reproduces the retinopathic side-effects of the antibiotic gentamicin.
source: In addition, we demonstrate the applicability of the RoC for drug testing, by reproducing the retinopathic side-effects of the anti-malaria drug chloroquine and the antibiotic gentamicin.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing increased cell death in the RoC after gentamicin treatment (Figure 8d-g).

claim: ROs of 180 days of age harbor matured photoreceptors which have simple forms of inner and outer segments.
source: In order to reach a suitable maturation, ROs were differentiated for 180 days. ROs of that age harbor matured photoreceptors which have simple forms of inner and outer segments, situated on the surface of the ROs, visible in bright field microscopy or by immunostaining of respective markers (Figure 2b–f).
evidence: The claim is supported by bright field microscopy and immunostaining data shown in Figure 2b-f.

claim: ROs contain a mixed population of rods and cones.
source: Immunostaining of the respective organoids demonstrates the presence of a mixed population of rods and cones, identified by specific markers (rhodopsin for rods and Arrestin-3 for cones, Figure 2c–e, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data showing rhodopsin (rod marker) and Arrestin-3 (cone marker) in Figure 2c-e and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: ROM1 is a specific outer segment marker.
source: In order to analyze segment formation, we used ROM1 as it has been previously shown as specific outer segment marker (Datta et al., 2015) and verified the segment specificity by co-staining with the rod marker rhodopsin (Figure 2c–d,f).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Datta et al., 2015) and by co-staining data shown in Figure 2c-d,f.

claim: PNA lectin labels both rod and cone photoreceptor segments in ROs.
source: Further, we tested the previously described protein PNA lectin, which was delineated to specifically bind to cone photoreceptor segments (Blanks and Johnson, 1984). Co-staining of rhodopsin with PNA lectin exhibited that not only cone but also rod segments in ROs are labeled with PNA lectin (Figure 2e).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-staining data showing PNA lectin labeling both rhodopsin-positive (rod) and rhodopsin-negative (cone) segments in Figure 2e.

claim: The RoC consists of two transparent and biocompatible polymer layers.
source: Each RoC features four identical micro-tissues connected via a microchannel and is comprised of two transparent and biocompatible polymer layers.
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the RoC fabrication in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The top layer of the RoC features the compartments for the ROs and RPE.
source: The top layer features the compartments for the ROs and RPE, whereas the bottom layer provides a channel for a vasculature-like perfusion enabling a constant supply of nutrients and compounds.
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the RoC structure in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 3b.

claim: The bottom layer of the RoC provides a channel for a vasculature-like perfusion enabling a constant supply of nutrients and compounds.
source: The top layer features the compartments for the ROs and RPE, whereas the bottom layer provides a channel for a vasculature-like perfusion enabling a constant supply of nutrients and compounds.
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the RoC structure in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 3b.

claim: Both layers of the RoC are separated by a thin porous membrane mimicking the endothelial barrier.
source: Both layers are separated by a thin porous membrane mimicking the endothelial barrier and shielding the tissues from shear forces while simultaneously enabling the exchange of nutrients and metabolites (Figure 3b).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the RoC structure in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 3b.

claim: The porous membrane in the RoC shields the tissues from shear forces while simultaneously enabling the exchange of nutrients and metabolites.
source: Both layers are separated by a thin porous membrane mimicking the endothelial barrier and shielding the tissues from shear forces while simultaneously enabling the exchange of nutrients and metabolites (Figure 3b).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational fluid dynamics simulations shown in Figure 5 and the description of the membrane function.

claim: A stable tissue comprising ROs and RPE was achieved by first seeding hiPSC-derived RPE cells at a defined density into each tissue compartment and subsequent culture for 24 hr.
source: A stable tissue comprising ROs and RPE was achieved by first seeding hiPSC-derived RPE cells at a defined density into each tissue compartment (Figure 3c) and subsequent culture for 24 hr (Figure 3d).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the RoC assembly process and images shown in Figure 3c-d.

claim: ROs embedded in a hyaluronic acid-based hydrogel were injected into the tissue compartments after RPE seeding.
source: This step was followed by injection of ROs embedded in a hyaluronic acid-based hydrogel (representing the major component of the interphotoreceptor matrix between RPE and PRC) into the tissue compartments (Figure 3e).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the RoC assembly process and images shown in Figure 3e.

claim: The hyaluronic acid-based hydrogel represents the major component of the interphotoreceptor matrix between RPE and photoreceptors.
source: This step was followed by injection of ROs embedded in a hyaluronic acid-based hydrogel (representing the major component of the interphotoreceptor matrix between RPE and PRC) into the tissue compartments (Figure 3e).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the composition of the interphotoreceptor matrix.

claim: The hydrogel layer generates a defined distance between RPE cells and the outer limiting membrane of the ROs.
source: This led to the formation of a thin hydrogel layer, generating a defined distance between RPE cells and the outer limiting membrane of the ROs.
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the RoC assembly and by imaging data showing the distance between RPE and RO (Figure 6c).

claim: The hydrogel layer prevents direct contact and uncontrolled outgrowth of cells from the ROs during culture.
source: Thereby, a direct contact and, thus, an uncontrolled outgrowth of cells from the ROs during culture was successfully avoided.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing preserved OLM integrity and no cell outgrowth (Figure 6d).

claim: The controlled culture conditions enabled a stable culture of the RoC for at least 21 days.
source: The controlled culture conditions enabled a stable culture of the RoC for at least 21 days (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing RoC viability over 21 days in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: RPE in the RoC expresses the markers PAX6 and MITF after 7–14 days in the chip.
source: Expression of RPE markers PAX6 and MITF can be observed after 7–14 days in the chip (Figure 4a–b).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4a-b.

claim: Mature RPE inside the chip displayed cobble stone-like morphology and tight-junction formation.
source: Mature RPE inside the chip displayed cobble stone-like morphology and tight-junction formation visualized by ZO-1 staining (Figure 4c).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data showing ZO-1 in Figure 4c.

claim: The melanosome and pigmentation marker Melanoma gp100 was highly expressed in chip-cultured RPE.
source: The melanosome and pigmentation marker Melanoma gp100 (also called PMEL17 or Silver locus protein) (Berson et al., 2001; Theos et al., 2005) was highly expressed in chip-cultured RPE (Figure 4d) indicating a strong pigmentation.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4d and citations to published literature (Berson et al., 2001; Theos et al., 2005).

claim: Electron microscopy analysis revealed the presence of apical microvilli as well as a basal membrane in RPE after 7 days of on-chip culture.
source: Electron microscopy analysis revealed not only the strong pigmentation of the RPE but also the presence of apical microvilli as well as a basal membrane already after 7 days of on-chip culture (Figure 4e).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Polarized RPE displayed the polarized expression of ezrin, an apical microvilli marker.
source: Further, we observed the polarized expression of ezrin, an apical microvilli marker (Kivelä et al., 2000) (Figure 4f).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4f and a citation to published literature (Kivelä et al., 2000).

claim: Polarized RPE displayed basal secretion of VEGF-A.
source: Finally, polarized RPE displayed basal secretion of VEGF-A, which could be measured on-chip by using a double-channel chip in which basal and apical medium could be collected separately (Figure 4g).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: The VEGF-A concentration was higher in the basal channel than in the apical channel (70 vs 40 pg per chip in 24 hr).
source: The VEGF-A concentration was higher in the basal channel than in the apical (70 vs 40 pg per chip in 24 hr).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: The RPE in the RoC is strongly pigmented, polarized, and expresses respective RPE markers.
source: Taken together, the RPE in the RoC is strongly pigmented, polarized, and expresses respective RPE markers.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by multiple pieces of data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Due to the fluidic resistance of the porous membrane, the convective fluid flow is confined to the media channels.
source: Due to the fluidic resistance of the porous membrane, the convective fluid flow is confined to the media channels (Figure 5a).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational fluid dynamics simulations shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Nutrients, compounds, and further dissolved molecules are transported to the tissue chamber via diffusion.
source: At the same time, nutrients, compounds, and further dissolved molecules are transported to the tissue chamber via diffusion. This rapid process enables a precisely controllable delivery (Figure 5b) as well as a controlled washout.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational fluid dynamics simulations shown in Figure 5b.

claim: A complete distribution of dye was observed within 300 s at a flow rate of 20 µl/hr.
source: In order to verify this, we conducted a proof of concept experiment during which we switched from a colorless liquid to a colored one and observed a complete distribution of the dye within 300 s (flow rate of 20 µl/hr) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: TGF-β1 stimulation led to a 2-fold increase of VEGF-A levels in the effluent medium after 2 hr.
source: Already after 2 hr, we could observe a 2-fold increase of VEGF-A levels in the effluent medium relative to the baseline level at 0 hr.
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The washout of TGF-β1 using normal media led to a steady decrease of VEGF-A levels at the 36 and 48 hr time-point.
source: The subsequent washout of TGF-β1 using normal media led to a steady decrease of VEGF-A levels at the 36 and 48 hr time-point, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The close proximity and the precisely orchestrated interaction of photoreceptors and the RPE layer is fundamental for vision.
source: The close proximity and the precisely orchestrated interaction of photoreceptors and the RPE layer is fundamental for vision, ensuring the phagocytosis and processing of shed photoreceptor outer segments (POS) as well as a supply of nutrients and oxygen (Elman et al., 1976).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Elman et al., 1976) and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: The RoC device allows the establishment of a defined interaction site between the segment structures of the RO and RPE cells without impairing neither structure nor viability of the organoid.
source: The RoC device allows the establishment of a defined interaction site between the segment structures of the RO and RPE cells without impairing neither structure nor viability of the organoid (Figure 6—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing preserved retinal markers and low cell death in Figure 6—figure supplements 1–2.

claim: The distance between lectin-marked segment tips and GFP-labeled RPE was approximately 5 ± 3.19 µm.
source: By measuring the distance between lectin-marked segment tips and GFP-labeled RPE, we found a distance of approximately 5 ± 3.19 µm over different experiments (Figure 6c).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurement data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Immunostaining revealed that the segment structures and RPE cells are in close apposition on-chip.
source: Subsequently, immunostaining using rhodopsin (rod outer segments) and phalloidin (cytoskeleton of the RPE and the RO including tight junctions) revealed that the segment structures and RPE cells are in close apposition on-chip (Figure 6b).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: After 7 days of on-chip culture, the close proximity of RPE and RO was preserved and no indication of cell outgrowth or general loss of integrity of the continuous OLM was observed.
source: After 7 days of on-chip culture, the close proximity of RPE and RO was preserved and no indication of cell outgrowth or general loss of integrity of the continuous OLM, labeled by the actin-cytoskeleton marker phalloidin, was observed (Figure 6d).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: The hydrogel-filled space between the RPE monolayer and the RO was strongly invaded by rhodopsin and ROM1-positive clusters indicating an increased and cumulated presence of inner and outer segment-like structures.
source: Further, the hydrogel-filled space between the RPE monolayer and the RO was strongly invaded by rhodopsin and ROM1 (outer segment marker)-positive clusters indicating an increased and cumulated presence of inner and outer segment-like structures (Figure 6d).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Electron microscopy confirmed the formation of numerous inner segments with clusters of mitochondria as well as the maintenance of the OLM.
source: A detailed analysis of the interaction site via electron microscopy confirmed the formation of numerous inner segments with clusters of mitochondria as well as the maintenance of the OLM (Figure 6e).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 6e.

claim: In the RoC system, the number of outer segment structures was about three times higher than in RO chips without RPE and in dish cultured ROs.
source: However, in the RoC system (RoC), the number of outer segment structures was about three times higher than in RO chips without RPE (RoC w/o RPE) and in dish cultured ROs (Figure 6h).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6h.

claim: There was no difference observed in the number of outer segments in the RoC chip without RPE and dish culture, indicating a positive effect of the RPE on outer segment formation and preservation.
source: Interestingly, there was no difference observed in the RoC chip without RPE and dish culture, indicating a positive effect of the RPE on outer segment formation and preservation.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6h and represents an inference from the data.

claim: The RoC increases the formation of outer segment-like structures on the RO without disturbing the normal survival and makeup of the organoid structure.
source: In summary, the RoC increases the formation of outer segment-like structures on the RO without disturbing the normal survival and makeup of the organoid structure.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplements 1–2.

claim: Calcium ions (Ca2+) are fundamentally important for the function of photoreceptors and involved in many processes ranging from photodetection, transduction and synaptic transfer.
source: Calcium ions (Ca2+) are fundamentally important for the function of photoreceptors and involved in many processes ranging from photodetection, transduction and synaptic transfer (reviewed in Krizaj and Copenhagen, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a review article (Krizaj and Copenhagen, 2002) and represents established knowledge.

claim: The general capability of the hiPSC-RPE to perform phagocytosis was verified using bovine retinal outer segments.
source: The general capability of the hiPSC-RPE to perform phagocytosis was initially verified using bovine retinal outer segments (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Already after 1 day in culture, PNA lectin-positive structures were found within the RPE cell bodies, indicating ongoing digestion of segment particles.
source: Already after 1 day in culture, PNA lectin-positive structures were found within the RPE cell bodies, indicating ongoing digestion of segment particles (Figure 7a).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: Many of the lectin-positive particles found in the RPE cells were positive for rhodopsin.
source: This revealed that many of the lectin-positive particles found in the RPE cells were positive for rhodopsin.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Specific co-localization of GFP-labeled early endosomes with rhodopsin-positive fragments was detected.
source: After on-chip immunostaining of rhodopsin, specific co-localization of GFP-labeled early endosomes with rhodopsin-positive fragments was detected (Figure 7c).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7c.

claim: Electron microscopy revealed several membrane stack-structures in the RPE below the RO that displayed multi-membrane formation as well as small round membrane structures, strongly reminiscent of similar features found in outer segment-like structures in ROs.
source: Here, we found several membrane stack-structures in the RPE below the RO. These structures displayed multi-membrane formation (red arrow) as well as small round membrane structures, both strongly reminiscent of similar features found in outer segment-like structures in ROs (Figure 7d, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7d.

claim: The findings strongly indicate functional indigestion of segment structures by the RPE, which is a major prerequisite for a functional visual cycle and therefore a physiological RPE-photoreceptor model.
source: Taken together, this strongly indicates functional indigestion of segment structures by the RPE, which is a major prerequisite for a functional visual cycle and therefore a physiological RPE-photoreceptor model.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement based on inference from the phagocytosis data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Chloroquine was previously shown to have pathological side effects on the retina.
source: In order to highlight the RoC's applicability for drug development and toxicology assessment, we exposed the system to the anti-malaria drug chloroquine (CQ) and the antibiotic gentamicin (GM), which both were previously shown to have pathological side effects on the retina (Elman et al., 1976; Ding et al., 2016; Yusuf et al., 2017; Zemel et al., 1995; McDonald et al., 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Elman et al., 1976; Ding et al., 2016; Yusuf et al., 2017; Zemel et al., 1995; McDonald et al., 1986).

claim: Gentamicin was previously shown to have pathological side effects on the retina.
source: In order to highlight the RoC's applicability for drug development and toxicology assessment, we exposed the system to the anti-malaria drug chloroquine (CQ) and the antibiotic gentamicin (GM), which both were previously shown to have pathological side effects on the retina (Elman et al., 1976; Ding et al., 2016; Yusuf et al., 2017; Zemel et al., 1995; McDonald et al., 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Elman et al., 1976; Ding et al., 2016; Yusuf et al., 2017; Zemel et al., 1995; McDonald et al., 1986).

claim: When RoCs were exposed to 20 µg/ml CQ, no significant impact on cell viability and only a minor increase in LAMP2 signal were observed.
source: When RoCs were exposed to 20 µg/ml CQ, no significant impact on cell viability (Figure 8b) and only a minor increase in LAMP2 signal (Figure 8c) were observed.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8b-c.

claim: At a concentration of 80 µg/ml CQ, cell viability was clearly impacted as shown by a significantly stronger PI staining compared to controls without CQ treatment.
source: However, at a concentration of 80 µg/ml, cell viability was clearly impacted as shown by a significantly stronger PI staining (Figure 8a,b) compared to controls without CQ treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8a-b.

claim: After exposure to 80 µg/ml CQ, a strong LAMP2 signal was visible, indicating an enlargement of lysosomes where the drug is accumulating and leading to lysosomal dysfunction.
source: Furthermore, after exposure to 80 µg/ml CQ, a strong LAMP2 signal was visible (Figure 8c), indicating an enlargement of lysosomes where the drug is accumulating and leading to lysosomal dysfunction.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8c and by inference based on known mechanisms of chloroquine toxicity.

claim: Lysosomal dysfunction is involved in the pathophysiology of chloroquine toxicity.
source: Additionally, they were co-stained with the lysosomal marker protein LAMP2 (Figure 8c) since lysosomal dysfunction is involved in the pathophysiology of CQ (Chen et al., 2011; Mahon et al., 2004; Rosenthal et al., 1978).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Chen et al., 2011; Mahon et al., 2004; Rosenthal et al., 1978).

claim: The increase in LAMP2 after CQ treatment was not limited to the RPE but was also very pronounced in the RO.
source: The increase in LAMP2 was not limited to the RPE but was also very pronounced in the RO (Figure 8c).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8c.

claim: In RoCs without RPE, an increase in cell death was observed at a GM concentration of 0.5 mg/ml.
source: In RoCs without RPE, an increase in cell death was observed at a GM concentration of 0.5 mg/ml (Figure 8f) and even more prominent in RoCs exposed to a 5-fold higher GM concentration (2.5 mg/ml), which was significant in comparison to the controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8f.

claim: In RoCs without RPE, exposure to 2.5 mg/ml GM led to a significant increase in cell death compared to controls.
source: In RoCs without RPE, an increase in cell death was observed at a GM concentration of 0.5 mg/ml (Figure 8f) and even more prominent in RoCs exposed to a 5-fold higher GM concentration (2.5 mg/ml), which was significant in comparison to the controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8f.

claim: In the complete RoC (RO and RPE), low GM concentrations led to a profound yet not significant increase in the PI signal, whereas the high concentration of 2.5 mg/ml GM led to a significant strong increase.
source: In the complete RoC (RO and RPE), similar effects became apparent: The low GM concentrations led to a profound yet not significant increase in the PI signal, whereas the high concentration of 2.5 mg/ml GM led to a significant strong increase (Figure 8g).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8g.

claim: There was an increase of PI in the RO condition without RPE, but an unchanged PI signal in the RoC-cultured RO when treated with 0.5 mg/ml GM.
source: Interestingly, we found an increase of PI in the condition without RPE, but an unchanged PI signal in the RoC-cultured RO. This is in contrast to the results from the RoC without RPE, where a robust increase was observed when treating the chip with 0.5 mg/ml GM (Figure 8h).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8h.

claim: The RPE may have a barrier or protective function, shielding the organoid from gentamicin and decreasing the toxic effects of the drug on the organoid.
source: This could indicate a barrier or even protective function of the RPE, shielding the organoid from the drug and decreasing the toxic effects of the drug on the organoid.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the differential response to gentamicin in RoCs with and without RPE (Figure 8h).

claim: Both the tight barrier function of the RPE layer as well as the melanin-binding of GM could be the source of the protective effect.
source: Both the tight barrier function of the RPE layer as well as the melanin-binding of GM (known to be protective in ocular pigmented vs. albino animals (Zemel et al., 1995) could be the source of this protective effect.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation supported by a citation to published literature (Zemel et al., 1995) about melanin-binding of gentamicin.

claim: The RoC successfully recapitulates side-effects of the anti-malaria drug chloroquine.
source: The applicability of the RoC for compound screening and toxicological studies was demonstrated by i) the successful recapitulation of side-effects of the anti-malaria drug chloroquine and ii) the mimicry of gentamicin-induced retinopathy revealing a protective effect of the RPE barrier.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by data shown in Figure 8a-c.

claim: The RoC mimics gentamicin-induced retinopathy revealing a protective effect of the RPE barrier.
